name: Pachamanca a la Olla (Andean Home Adaptation)
category: Home-pot adaptation of an earth-oven meal
imageAlt: Home-style pachamanca a la olla with seasoned meat, potatoes, corn and fava beans arranged on a serving platter
imageCredit: Photo: MiguelAlanCS, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Pachamanca a la olla adapts Peru's Andean earth-oven feast to a tightly covered home pot, steaming herb-marinated pork and chicken with potatoes, sweet potato, corn and fava beans.
lead: Huacatay, chincho and ají panca perfume meat and Andean crops in this carefully labeled pot adaptation of a communal Peruvian earth-oven tradition.
about: Peru's Ministry of Agrarian Development describes pachamanca as an Andean preparation of seasoned meats, potatoes, sweet potatoes, corn, fava beans and aromatic herbs cooked with preheated stones. The name is commonly explained through Quechua pacha, earth, and manka, pot. Traditional pachamanca is built in the ground and shared communally; pachamanca a la olla is a recognized domestic adaptation that creates a sealed, herb-scented cooking environment in a heavy pot without pretending to reproduce hot-stone cooking.
story: Official Peruvian sources treat pachamanca as both food and a relationship among people, land and agricultural products. Regional versions in Junín, Cusco, Ayacucho, Huánuco, Áncash and elsewhere use different meats, tubers, herbs and accompaniments, and the opening of an earth oven often belongs to harvests, festivals and family gatherings. This recipe follows the contemporary a-la-olla path documented in Peru: meat is marinated with ají and herbs, layered with crops in a lined pot and cooked by trapped steam. It is an invitation to learn the flavors, not a substitute for the collective knowledge or ceremonial setting of a community-made pachamanca.
caveat: Call this pachamanca a la olla, not traditional earth-oven pachamanca. Do not heat random river rocks in a kitchen oven or pot; trapped moisture can make unsuitable stones fracture violently. Huacatay and chincho are characteristic Andean aromatics. If chincho is unavailable, use additional huacatay and oregano while noting the flavor change. Regional pachamancas vary widely, so the chicken-and-pork combination here is one practical version rather than a universal formula.
prepNotes: Give the meat at least 8 hours in the herb and ají mixture. The seasoning should reach every surface before the pot is packed.
A heavy 6- to 8-quart Dutch oven and a tight layer of foil beneath the lid mimic the enclosed cooking environment better than a loose stockpot lid.
The corn-husk lining adds aroma and keeps the food organized, but it does not create the mineral heat or communal process of a stone-lined pit.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb boneless pork shoulder, cut into 2-inch pieces
2 lb bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks
1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, divided, plus more to taste
1/3 cup ají panca paste
5 garlic cloves, finely grated
1 tsp ground cumin
1/2 tsp freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup packed huacatay leaves, or 3 tbsp jarred huacatay paste
1/4 cup packed chincho leaves, or 2 tbsp additional huacatay plus 1 tsp dried oregano
1/2 cup chicha de jora or a mild lager
2 tbsp red-wine vinegar
1 tbsp neutral oil
1 1/2 lb small yellow or purple potatoes, scrubbed
1 lb sweet potatoes, scrubbed and cut into 2-inch pieces
2 ears corn, shucked and cut crosswise into thirds
8 oz fresh fava beans in their pods, rinsed, or 1 1/2 cups shelled fava beans
8 oz queso fresco, cut into 6 thick slices, optional
12 to 16 dried corn husks, soaked until pliable, or food-safe banana leaves
1/2 cup water, plus more only if needed
steps: Blend the ají panca, garlic, cumin, pepper, huacatay, chincho, chicha, vinegar, oil and 1 teaspoon salt into a loose green-red paste. If using jarred herb paste, check its salt before adding the full amount.

Rub the marinade thoroughly over the pork and chicken, working it beneath any loose chicken skin. Cover and refrigerate at least 8 hours and up to 24 hours; keep the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt for the vegetables.

Thirty minutes before cooking, remove the meat from the refrigerator. Drain the softened corn husks and use them to line the bottom and sides of a heavy 6- to 8-quart Dutch oven, leaving enough overhang to fold across the top.

Season the potatoes, sweet potatoes, corn and fava pods with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt. Arrange the pork in one layer over the husks, set the chicken skin-side up around it and scrape all remaining marinade over the meat.

Layer the potatoes and sweet potatoes over and around the meat, followed by the corn and fava beans. Pour 1/2 cup water down the side of the pot rather than washing seasoning from the surface. Tuck in the optional queso fresco where it will not sit directly on the pot bottom.

Fold the corn husks or banana leaves over the food. Press a sheet of heavy foil directly beneath the lid to make a tight seal. Bring the pot just to a lively steam over medium heat, about 8 minutes, then immediately reduce the heat to low.
Cook without opening for 70 minutes. Listen for a quiet steady simmer; aggressive boiling can scorch the lower layer, while complete silence after the first 15 minutes may mean the heat is too low.

Open carefully away from your face. Checkpoint: the chicken must register at least 165°F at the thickest part, pork should be fork-tender, and a thin knife should slide through the potatoes and sweet potatoes without resistance. Reseal and cook 15 to 25 minutes longer if any component is firm.

Transfer the cooked meat and vegetables to a warm platter. If more than 1 cup thin liquid remains, simmer it uncovered for 5 to 8 minutes until lightly concentrated; if the pot is nearly dry but nothing is scorched, simply spoon the aromatic juices over the platter.

Rest the meat 10 minutes, then serve family-style with the potatoes, sweet potatoes, corn, fava beans and optional cheese. Explain at the table that this is the home-pot form; a traditional pachamanca is cooked collectively with heated stones in the earth.
Cool leftovers in shallow containers within 2 hours. Reheat covered until the meat reaches 165°F and the tubers are steaming through.

name: Southern Thai Khao Yam (Herbal Rice Salad)
type: Rice Salad / Breakfast or Light Meal
category: Herbal rice salad with budu dressing
imageAlt: Southern Thai khao yam served unmixed with rice, pomelo, bean sprouts, finely cut herbs, toasted coconut and dried shrimp
imageCredit: Photo: Takeaway, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Southern Thai khao yam combines cooled rice with finely cut herbs, crisp vegetables, pomelo, toasted coconut and dried shrimp, tossed at the table with sweet-salty aromatic budu dressing.
lead: Every component stays distinct until the last moment, when rice, herbs, fruit, coconut and a measured spoonful of fragrant budu sauce are tossed into one bright southern Thai meal.
about: The MICHELIN Guide and Thai culinary archive Ros Chaad Thai describe khao yam, also called khao yam budu, as a southern Thai rice salad balancing rice, herbs and vegetables, toasted coconut, dried seafood and nam budu, a seasoned fermented-fish dressing. Thai dictionary sources write the name ข้าวยำ and define it through the action of mixing cooked rice with finely cut accompaniments. This version keeps the budu sauce separate until serving so each diner can balance its saltiness against the rice, pomelo and herbs.
story: Khao yam belongs to the food culture of Thailand's south and shares a borderland conversation with Malay nasi kerabu, but the two should not be collapsed into one recipe. Southern Thai plates may use white, brown or naturally colored rice and change with available herbs, fruit and vegetables. Budu is the anchor: it is simmered with aromatics and palm sugar, then used sparingly to bind many fresh textures. The dish is commonly eaten for breakfast or lunch and rewards precise knife work more than heavy cooking.
caveat: Budu varies in salt and fermentation intensity, so taste a cooled drop before dressing the salad and never pour in the entire batch automatically. Fish sauce mixed with shrimp paste can approximate salinity and umami when budu is truly unavailable, but it is not the same fermented ingredient and should be labeled as a substitute. Khao yam is assembled flexibly; the aim is a deliberate mixture of rice, aromatic leaves, crisp vegetables, fruit, toasted coconut and seafood seasoning rather than a fixed rainbow garnish list.
prepNotes: Makrut lime leaf and lemongrass remain tough when thick. Remove hard ribs and outer layers, then slice into nearly hair-thin threads.
Warm rice wilts the herbs and turns the salad heavy. Spread it on a tray until no steam remains, then cover so it does not dry out.
Treat budu like a concentrated dressing
Different brands have different salt levels. Begin with 1 tablespoon per serving, toss completely and add more only after tasting.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups jasmine rice, rinsed until the water is mostly clear
2 cups water, or the amount required by the rice package
1/2 cup bottled southern Thai or Malaysian budu fermented fish sauce
3/4 cup water, for the dressing
2 stalks lemongrass, lower tender portions bruised and cut into 2-inch pieces
1 inch galangal, sliced
2 small shallots, crushed
3 makrut lime leaves, torn and center ribs removed
1 pandan leaf, knotted, optional
1/3 cup finely chopped palm sugar, plus more to balance
1 tbsp tamarind concentrate or 2 tbsp fresh lime juice, as needed
3/4 cup unsweetened shredded coconut
1/3 cup dried shrimp, ground fluffy in a spice grinder or mortar
1 cup bean sprouts, rinsed and dried
1 cup yard-long beans or green beans, sliced very thin
1 cup pomelo segments, membranes removed and pulp broken into small pieces
1 small firm sour mango, peeled and finely julienned, or 1 tart green apple
1 small cucumber, seeded and finely julienned
2 tender lemongrass stalks, outer layers removed and sliced paper-thin
6 makrut lime leaves, center ribs removed and cut into hair-thin threads
1/2 cup packed wild betel leaves or mint leaves, sliced thin
1/2 cup finely sliced cilantro and scallions
Roasted chile flakes, for serving
6 lime wedges, for serving
steps: Cook the rinsed rice with 2 cups water according to the package directions. Rest covered 10 minutes, fluff gently, then spread on a rimmed tray until completely cool and the grains separate without feeling dry.

Combine budu, 3/4 cup water, bruised lemongrass, galangal, shallots, torn makrut leaves, optional pandan and palm sugar in a small saucepan. Bring to a gentle boil, skimming any foam, then lower the heat.

Simmer the dressing 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the palm sugar dissolves and the liquid smells rounded and aromatic rather than sharply fishy. Strain through a fine sieve and cool before judging its balance.

Checkpoint: cooled budu dressing should pour easily, taste distinctly salty and sweet, and carry lemongrass and galangal in the aroma. Add tamarind or lime a little at a time for a light sour edge; thin with water if it is syrupy or overwhelmingly salty.

Toast the coconut in a dry skillet over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until deep brown and nutty rather than merely pale gold, 6 to 10 minutes. Transfer immediately to a plate so residual pan heat does not burn it.
Toast the ground dried shrimp in the same dry skillet for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until fragrant and a shade darker. Cool completely. Keep it separate from the coconut for serving.

Prepare the bean sprouts, beans, pomelo, mango, cucumber, tender lemongrass, makrut leaves, wild betel or mint, cilantro and scallions. Keep wet ingredients drained and blot the herbs dry so they do not dilute the salad.
Checkpoint: the lemongrass and makrut leaf should be fine enough that no strip feels woody when chewed. Re-slice any coarse pieces before they reach the platter.

Arrange the cool rice in the center of a large platter and place the vegetables, fruit, herbs, toasted coconut and dried shrimp in separate piles around it. Serve the cooled budu dressing, chile flakes and lime wedges alongside.

For each serving, start with about 1 cup rice and a generous handful of every fresh component. Add 1 tablespoon budu dressing and toss thoroughly until the herbs and coconut are distributed through the rice; taste before adding more dressing, chile or lime.
Assemble only what will be eaten immediately. Refrigerate extra rice, dressing and cut components separately; use the fresh herbs within 1 day and the dressing within 1 week.

difficultyReason: Requires simmering and balancing a concentrated budu dressing while finely slicing many herbs and coordinating several toasted and fresh components.

name: Armenian Zhingyalov Hats (Herb-Stuffed Flatbread)
region: Armenian communities of Artsakh and Syunik / South Caucasus
type: Stuffed Flatbread / Snack or Light Meal
imageAlt: Armenian zhingyalov hats cut open to show a dense filling of finely chopped greens inside thin griddled dough
imageCredit: Photo: Արարատ Թրվանց, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Armenian zhingyalov hats encloses a generous mixture of neutral, aromatic and sour greens in paper-thin unleavened dough, sealed into pointed flatbreads and cooked on a dry griddle.
lead: The dough is deliberately spare so the greens lead: spinach and chard give body, herbs supply perfume, and sorrel or watercress brings the sour edge that keeps the filling vivid.
about: A Smithsonian cooking demonstration based on the cookbook Lavash presents zhingyalov hats as a thin Armenian flatbread packed with a carefully balanced mixture of greens and herbs. Armenian usage literally describes bread with zhengyal, a dialect word for herbs or greens. The dish is particularly associated with Armenian communities from Artsakh and Syunik. A home skillet replaces the large saj griddle, but the essential method remains: roll unleavened dough thin, enclose a substantial raw herb filling, seal it securely and cook it dry until blistered.
story: The abundance of greens is not decorative. Cooks build the filling from several roles: mild leaves form the bulk, aromatic herbs add intensity, and sour or peppery greens keep the mixture lively. The exact plants change with season, place and family knowledge, and Armenian cooks may use far more wild and cultivated greens than a supermarket version can reproduce. Contemporary Armenian restaurants in the diaspora preserve that flexibility; the MICHELIN Guide records a Glendale bakery using more than a dozen varieties while emphasizing that families do not share one mandatory formula.
caveat: Spellings including zhingyalov hats, zhengyalov hatz and jingalov hats represent the same Armenian name in Latin letters. This recipe uses cultivated greens that are realistic and safe for a North American kitchen; do not forage unfamiliar wild plants to imitate a longer traditional list. Qutab and gözleme are neighboring filled-flatbread traditions, but their dough, shapes, fillings and serving contexts should not be treated as interchangeable with this Armenian dish.
prepNotes: Wash greens well ahead and dry them completely. Surface water steams the dough, makes sealing difficult and leaves the interior soggy.
Use roughly half mild leaves, one quarter aromatic herbs and one quarter sour or peppery leaves rather than letting one assertive herb dominate.
Salt draws water from chopped greens quickly. Mix it in after the dough is rolled and cook each filled bread without delay.
ingredients: 1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting
1 tsp kosher salt
2/3 cup lukewarm water, plus 1 to 2 tbsp only if needed
4 packed cups baby spinach and thinly sliced Swiss chard
1 packed cup finely sliced flat-leaf parsley
1/2 packed cup finely chopped dill
1/2 packed cup finely chopped cilantro or chervil
1 packed cup finely sliced sorrel, watercress or peppery arugula
3 scallions, white and green parts thinly sliced
1 tsp sweet paprika
1/2 tsp Aleppo pepper or mild red-pepper flakes
1 1/2 tbsp sunflower or neutral oil
1 tbsp fresh lemon juice
3/4 tsp kosher salt, for the filling
Plain yogurt, tan or lemon wedges, optional for serving
steps: Dissolve 1 teaspoon salt in the lukewarm water. Add the flour and mix until no dry patches remain, adding up to 2 tablespoons more water only if the dough will not come together.

Knead on a lightly floured surface for 5 to 7 minutes, until smooth and elastic. Cover and rest 25 to 40 minutes. Checkpoint: a pressed indentation should relax slowly, and the dough should roll without springing immediately back.
While the dough rests, stack and slice all greens and herbs very fine. Spread them briefly on a clean towel and blot again; the mixture should feel leafy and dry rather than wet or compacted.

Combine the mild greens, aromatic herbs, sour or peppery greens and scallions in a very large bowl. Leave the paprika, Aleppo pepper, oil, lemon juice and filling salt separate until the first dough round is ready.

Divide the rested dough into 4 equal balls and keep three covered. Roll one ball on a floured surface into an 8- to 9-inch circle, turning often, until it is about 1/16 inch thick and faintly translucent without holes.

Toss the entire greens mixture with paprika, Aleppo pepper, oil, lemon juice and 3/4 teaspoon salt. Use your hands to distribute the seasoning without crushing the leaves. Divide the filling visually into four portions.

Mound one portion of greens down the center of the dough, leaving a 1-inch border. Bring the left and right edges together over the filling and pinch from one pointed end to the other, expelling large air pockets as you go.

Turn the sealed bread seam-side down and press gently with your palms into a flattened oval about 1/3 inch thick. Checkpoint: greens should reach the pointed ends, the seam should remain closed and no stem should pierce the dough.

Heat a large dry cast-iron skillet or griddle over medium-high heat. Lay in the bread seam-side down, reduce to medium and cook 2 1/2 to 3 minutes, until the underside has browned spots and releases easily.

Flip and cook 2 to 3 minutes more. Press lightly around any pale areas and turn once or twice as needed. The finished dough should be cooked through and flexible with scattered dark blisters; the greens inside should be collapsed, aromatic and still bright rather than watery.

Repeat with the remaining dough and filling, wiping loose flour from the skillet between breads so it does not burn. Keep finished flatbreads under a clean towel for a softer surface or on a rack for a slightly crisper one.
Serve warm or at room temperature, whole or cut into strips, with optional yogurt, tan or lemon. Cool leftovers completely before wrapping; refrigerate up to 2 days and reheat in a dry skillet.
